alerts.title: DTG-associated hyperglycemia risk with pre-diabetes
alerts.message: Guidelines require glucose screening for clients transitioning to DTG who have ≥2 hyperglycemia risk factors (age ≥30, family history of DM, BMI ≥25). This patient has all three. DTG has been associated with hyperglycemia in previously non-diabetic adults. Patient now has fasting glucose 118 mg/dL (impaired) and HbA1c 6.1% (pre-diabetic) after 18 months on DTG, up from baseline fasting glucose of 92 mg/dL. Acanthosis nigricans further supports insulin resistance. Evidence for drug attribution: new-onset dysglycemia temporally follows DTG initiation with known pharmacologic association. Evidence against: family history of DM and obesity are independent risk factors. Guidelines recommend RBS every 3 months for high-risk patients in the first 12 months; no glucose monitoring appears to have been done during that period.

evidence.recommended_action: Assess whether DTG should be continued versus switched given pre-diabetes progression. Initiate lifestyle modification. Monitor fasting glucose and HbA1c every 3 months. Consider metformin if progression continues.

alerts.title: Significant weight gain and obesity on DTG
alerts.message: Guidelines identify obesity as a preventable disorder increasing risk of heart disease and diabetes. Patient gained 17kg (65kg to 82kg) with BMI rising from 25.6 to 32.4 kg/m² over 18 months on DTG, moving from normal to obese class I. Waist circumference 96cm indicates central adiposity. DTG is associated with weight gain compared to other ARVs. Evidence for drug attribution: rapid weight gain temporally coincides with DTG switch, and DTG-related weight gain is well documented. Evidence against: lifestyle factors, diet, and physical activity changes are not documented and could contribute. The compounding risk of obesity plus pre-diabetes plus dyslipidemia significantly increases cardiovascular and metabolic risk.

evidence.recommended_action: Counsel on lifestyle modification including diet and 30 minutes aerobic exercise daily ≥5 days/week. Consider DTG-related weight gain in regimen review. Address obesity as part of comprehensive metabolic risk reduction.

alerts.title: Elevated BP requires hypertension screening
alerts.message: Guidelines state all PLHIV should be screened for hypertension risk factors at every visit. Patient's BP today is 138/88 mmHg, up from baseline 118/74 mmHg. While not yet meeting the ≥140/90 threshold for pharmacologic treatment, this represents a significant upward trend. The hypertension treatment protocol indicates Step 1 management for BP ≥140-159/90-99 with <3 risk factors and no target organ damage. This patient has multiple cardiovascular risk factors including obesity, dyslipidemia, pre-diabetes, and family history of DM. No BP management plan was documented.

evidence.recommended_action: Repeat BP measurement to confirm. Initiate lifestyle modification. Monitor BP closely given multiple risk factors. If persistently ≥140/90, follow hypertension treatment protocol Step 1.

alerts.title: Significant dyslipidemia with atherogenic profile
alerts.message: Guidelines identify dyslipidemia as a hypertension risk factor requiring screening at every visit. Patient has total cholesterol 228 mg/dL, LDL 148 mg/dL, HDL 38 mg/dL, and triglycerides 212 mg/dL, representing a highly atherogenic lipid profile. This pattern—low HDL with elevated triglycerides—is characteristic of insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome. Combined with obesity, pre-diabetes, elevated BP, and family history of DM, this patient meets criteria for metabolic syndrome, substantially elevating cardiovascular risk. No lipid management plan was documented by the clinician.

evidence.recommended_action: Initiate dietary intervention and lifestyle modification. Consider fasting lipid panel repeat to confirm. Evaluate for pharmacologic lipid-lowering therapy given multiple cardiovascular risk factors and LDL ≥130.
